parts.why: One opinion and one reason sentence per piece; positions vary (A: 1st, 2nd; B: 2nd, 1st). Read aloud, so no reading demand.
Form A: 'A lion can roar.' is keyed X beside a cat, but a lion is a big cat, so a child can defend a check mark. B's X (whale) is plainly off-topic, so A is harder. Use 'A fish can swim.'
One order per story (A 1-3-2, B 2-3-1); events clearly sequenced.
One sentence answers each question; the two distractors answer other questions. Answer positions vary.

'Draw your favorite in the box': the page has two boxes (prompt box with dice/monkey, dotted box); say 'the big dotted box'. A favorite game (tag) is much harder to draw than B's animal: use 'My favorite food'. Two lines are tight for two K sentences with a quarter page empty: print three.

Both forms print the whole story in order (First…, Next…, Last…) right above the three sentences, so numbering is copying, not sequencing. Print the title and the three event sentences scrambled, with no ordered paragraph.

B card 2: 'They do not spill like paint.' is true of rockets; A card 2: 'They come in many shapes.' is half-true of frogs. Lures must be false of the topic ('They have soft fur.'). B's two answers are A's card-2 lures, so B repeats A.
'Now you know about bees/turtles!' is the only closing; positions differ (A 3rd, B 1st).
One error per sentence; A and B parallel (end mark, i, first letter). Key marks clear.
Best season / best recess game: same kind and load; six primary lines fit four short sentences. Seasons are weak in warm US regions, acceptable.

Both stories hold time phrases that do not tell order (A 'on Saturday'; B 'at recess on Friday'), which a G2 child calls time words. Direction: 'Circle the three words that tell the order (like First).' Say on the key whether 'After' alone earns the point.
One error each (name, first letter, end mark), parallel in A and B.
A time I helped a friend / tried something new: same kind; ten lines fit.
The opinion is the only sentence that does not belong in each card; facts true.

Both forms answer 'and' then 'another'; 'also' is never right, so a child scores 2/2 without 'also', the word the writing guide rewards. Make one card per form an 'also' gap ('Raccoons eat fruit. They ___ eat nuts.').

A's answers are Both, Both, Book 1 (no Book 2); B's are Book 2, Book 1, Both. Ticking 'Both' everywhere scores 2/3 in A, 1/3 in B. Give A a Book 2 note ('a short tail' or 'drink water from streams'). Facts check out.
Foxes/penguins: same facts load, each box holds one 'is called' fact for the definition. Facts true. See the definition point in the guide.
One opinion, one closing, three reasons each. Minor: A's opinion has no 'I think' (harder than B), and the opinion is letter B in both forms.
Only one option is a reason (the on-topic fact is true of all birds / not a reason). Positions vary.
Comma placement tested cleanly (L.2.2.b); positions vary.
Election Day, Juneteenth, Presidents' Day, Thanksgiving correct; 'fall' is a fair non-capital lure. Places and brand names, named in the lesson, are not checked.
Best recess game / best place in school to read: same kind, both give easy reasons; nine lines fit.
Each sentence clearly fact or opinion; 3 facts/3 opinions per form.

A card 1 needs fronted 'Since…,' (harder); B card 1 is mid-sentence 'because' (easier) and B offers 'because' where A offers 'since'. 'For example' is never right in either form. Make B card 1 a 'Since' sentence and one card per form a 'For example' gap.
The X sentence is identical in both forms ('Tomorrow we have a spelling test.'), so B repeats A. Give B its own off-topic line ('My cousin has a red bike.'). Keys otherwise right.
Form B 'we have field day': many US schools write 'Field Day', so a child may fix the capitals and miss the period, seeing two mistakes. Use 'we have a picnic'.
Field trip / class party: same three-choice shape and difficulty; fourteen lines fit.

A card 1: the sentence says rope bridges are still found in some mountains; the keyed note 'some made of rope' records a different idea and drops the point. Key 'rope bridges: some mountains', lure 'rope bridges: all mountains'.
Keys right, but B's notes say 'active: just erupted', a wrong definition (an active volcano erupts now or may erupt again). Use 'active: may erupt again'.

Every later sentence is also a fact, so 'Fact' is defensible on every row (A 'Each color bends a different amount.'), and 'One is called north…' reads as a definition. Print sentence 1 as the fact and ask only Definition or Detail; drop 'is called' from detail rows.
Beavers/honeybees: same three-heading notes; facts true (teeth keep growing, five eyes, six-sided cells).
One problem each. B's answer echoes the text ('one big tangle'), slightly easier than A; acceptable.
Inside/outside punctuation tested cleanly (L.3.2.c); positions vary.
One time word fits each blank; B card 2 tests a story opener, a fair variation.

B reuses A's words with roles swapped (shouted/whispered, tasty, marched, tall) and mirrors A's cards (good, said, went). Give B new tired words and choices ('big' → enormous; 'looked' → peeked; 'ate' → gobbled).

instruction.K-674: Your teacher reads the words at the top. Draw your favorite in the big dotted box. Then write what you like best and why.
instruction.G2-571: Read the true story. Circle the three words that tell the order of what happened (like First).
instruction.G3-560: Each part starts with a fact. For each sentence after it, put a check mark under definition or detail.
instruction.G3-569: Write a story about the idea. Introduce the characters, the setting, and the problem, tell the events in order with time words, show how a character feels with dialogue and an action, and write an ending.

worksheet: G3-511 water cycle (info-graphics-g3, diagrams[0]): 'What happens to the water during evaporation?' is now text-only, one answer. But the NEW both question 'What is the name of the step in which rain or snow falls?' can be answered from the diagram alone (the Precipitation box shows rain falling), so 'diagram' is defensible. Reword: 'What is the name of the step that comes when the drops in a cloud grow big and heavy?' (cue 'heavy', group heavy). Also: the text now names 'evaporation', against the type's own rule that only the diagram names the steps; any future question naming evaporation is text-only.
G3-556 Choose and Sort Notes, bridges: 'Rope bridges can still be found in some mountains.' is keyed 'some made of rope', which is not a note of that sentence. Key 'rope bridges: some mountains'.
G3-558 Introductions and Groups, volcano notes: 'active: just erupted' is a wrong definition; use 'active: may erupt again'.

G3-560 Fact, Definition, or Detail?: offering 'Fact' for the sentences after the first gives two defensible answers (every detail is also a fact), and 'One is called north, and one is called south.' reads as a definition. Ask only definition or detail after the given fact.
G1-618 Opinion or Reason?: the lure 'They do not spill like paint.' is true of rockets and 'They come in many shapes.' is half-true of frogs; lures must be false of the topic.
K-675 Facts and Labels: 'A lion can roar.' beside a cat picture is keyed 'not about the cat', but a lion is a (big) cat; use an animal that is not a cat.
G3-554 Edit an Opinion Paragraph: 'we have field day' invites a capital fix ('Field Day') as a second mistake; use a plain noun.
notes: Job 3 checks: K-652 (Duck's New Hat) OK: sad, happy and angry faces read as three different feelings, and 'She is so sad' gives one answer. G2-522 OK: 'a juice factory'. G1-576 OK: headings print on their own line. G2-578 bank 'A Cold Day Inside' reads naturally and has one answer per view (Lucy: outside; Arjun: building; Ms. Webb: moving games; nobody: too quiet); only the check excerpt is wrong.
All eight writing teacher pages say 'In a box that says to circle every shape…' in How to use: math wording on a writing check. Say 'circle every word' or drop the sentence.

Several Secure 'what next' cells are not steps but a later unit: K conventions, G2 Writing Stories ending, G2 Writing to Inform definition, G2 Opinion linking, G3 Opinion conventions, G3 Informative conventions (Nearly and Secure), G3 Narrative ending (a reading unit). Give a concrete next task in this unit.

Guide 'what next' names worksheets that do not exist: G2 Writing to Inform 'Closings, Definitions, and Linking Words' (G2-567 is 'Closing Sentences and Linking Words'); G3 Opinion 'Find the Opinion and the Reasons' (G3-548 'Opinions and Reasons'), 'Find the Concluding Statement' (G3-552 'Find the Conclusion'), 'Write a Concluding Statement' (G3-553 'Write a Conclusion'), 'Revise and Edit an Opinion Paragraph' (G3-554 'Edit an Opinion Paragraph').

K and G1 units promise opinions, facts and stories, but the writing part is opinion in both forms; facts and stories are only recognized in the cut parts. Say so on the teacher pages or rotate the genre.
The recess-game prompt recurs: K form A 'My favorite game', G1 form B 'best recess game', G2 form A 'best game to play at recess'.
Reading units: the generic per-row '(1)/(2)' marks exist only in the read-aloud text on the key; the child's rows in K parts 1 and 3 carry no numbers.

rubric.why: Levels clear (topic word / one-word label / a sentence); real K spelling. Put the printed frame words in quotes in 'next' ('My favorite … is').
W.K.1 asks only for the opinion; a reason starts at W.1.1. Keep the point (the unit teaches 'why') but mark it 'beyond the K standard' so a 0 is not read as below grade.

Nearly example 'one child standing on grass' does not show tag and reads as Not yet: draw two children. 'Fun' cannot be drawn, so Secure depends on the reason chosen; name the details that count: who, where, or what is happening.

The commonest K stage, first sounds with spaces ('M f g i t'), fits no level; the Not yet example does stand for first sounds. Not yet: random letters; Nearly: first (some last) sounds, spaces; Secure: most sounds, spaces, capital, end mark.

A separate 'This is about…' sentence goes beyond W.1.1, and teachers will split on 'I think fall is the best season.'; the Nearly example names fall. Secure: topic named, alone or inside the opinion; Nearly: topic unclear ('I think it is the best.').
A reason without 'because' ('Fall is the best. You can jump in leaves.') fits no level, and W.1.1 does not require 'because'. Secure: a reason that tells why, after because or in its own sentence.
'In new words' exceeds W.1.1's 'some sense of closure'; a word-for-word repeat or 'I hope you like fall too!' has no level. Secure: a closing that goes back to the opinion; Nearly: 'The end.'
Most / some / every is clear; capital I included (L.1.2).
Events in clear order with NO time words fit neither Not yet (no clear order) nor Nearly (one or a repeated time word). Nearly: in order, with none, one, or the same time word.
Named feeling vs feeling plus what it is about: clear, matches W.2.3.

Not yet 'stops after an event' and Secure 'how it turned out' overlap ('Then we put them all back.'). The Secure example's feeling also earns the feeling point. Secure: a sentence after the last event telling the result or a final feeling; say whether it may count twice.
Clear; names and I added at G2.
Fact first / title only / topic sentence: distinguishable.

Two facts joined by a linking word ('Foxes have bushy tails and pointed ears.') fit no level: Nearly needs no linking word, Secure three facts. Nearly: two or more facts with at most one link; Secure: three facts, at least two joined.

The facts box prints 'A baby fox is called a kit.'; say whether copying it scores Secure. Suggested: copied = Nearly, rewritten 'A kit is a baby fox.' = Secure (the lesson's Level 2). Secure 'next' is the Grade 3 unit, not a step.
Clear; 'next' names a nonexistent worksheet (see notes).
Clear.
Nearly example 'I think tag is the best.' names the choice, so teachers will split; use the description's own 'I think it is the best.' as the example.
None / one / two or three: clear.
Clear; a one-reason piece also loses here, acceptable.
A closing that does not restate the opinion ('Come play tag with us!') fits no level; W.2.1 asks only for a concluding statement. Place it explicitly (Secure).
Clear.
Levels clear, but 'next' sends teachers to 'Find the Opinion and the Reasons'; the worksheet is 'Opinions and Reasons' (G3-548).

'Each with a fact or an example' is W.4.1b; W.3.1b asks reasons that support the opinion. The Secure example's second reason has no example, so it is Nearly by its own rule. Secure: two+ supporting reasons, one with an example.
'Kinds' is undefined: is 'One reason… Another reason…' one kind? Is 'also'? Secure: at least two different linking words or phrases from because, since, therefore, for example, another reason.

A concluding statement that does not restate the opinion has no level (W.3.1d asks only for one). 'Next' names 'Find/Write a Concluding Statement'; the worksheets are 'Find the Conclusion' (G3-552) and 'Write a Conclusion' (G3-553).

A comma after a starting time word is L.5.2b. A piece without 'For example' has no Secure rule; correct commas with two missing end marks fits no level. Score capitals and end marks; count the 'For example' comma only if used.

W.3.2a asks only to introduce the topic, so 'This is about beavers.' (Nearly) meets it; the Secure example tells nothing the reader will learn and reads like Not yet's fact. Nearly: title or topic word; Secure: a sentence introducing the topic.
Mixed / one stray fact / grouped: distinguishable, matches W.3.2a.

'Detail' is undefined against 'fact': every note sentence is both, so teachers cannot agree a detail is present. Define it: a sentence that tells more about the fact just before it (the lodge has an underwater door).
Clear.
A comma after a starting phrase ('In summer,') is L.5.2b; a piece without a list has no rule for list commas. Score capitals and end marks, plus series commas when a list is written.

'No character is named' fails first-person stories with an unnamed narrator, which meet W.3.3a: say 'no narrator or character'. The direction never asks for a setting, yet Secure needs where or when: add it to the direction.
Events in order with no time words fit no level. Nearly: in order with no time words or one repeated.

Direction says 'dialogue or actions'; Secure needs dialogue AND an action or thought, so feelings shown through actions only, as told, fit no level. Align them (W.3.3b says 'and'): change the direction, and place 'action only' at Nearly.

Not yet 'stops in the middle' and Nearly 'stops suddenly' cannot be told apart. Not yet: problem not solved; Nearly: solved in a rush or turns to something new; Secure: solved with a closing thought or feeling.
No rule for a story without dialogue, and 'sentences run together' has no count (one run-on = 0?). Score end marks by most/every, and quotation punctuation only where dialogue appears.
